body:
Nothing unusual to report today: the scanner found zero cross-platform arbitrage opportunities, and the pricing that is on offer looks broadly coherent rather than mispriced. Kalshi's ladder of gold above $X on September 30, 2026 settlement contracts crosses 50/50 between the $4,330.99 strike (bid 0.54 / ask 0.57) and the $4,370.99 strike (bid 0.45 / ask 0.49), putting the market's implied fair value right around $4,350. That lines up with where gold has actually been trading: Trading Economics had spot near $4,348 on September 11, 2026, up 0.71% on the day and still 19.34% higher than a year earlier, after a rally that pushed the metal decisively above the $4,000 mark this year. A separate outlook piece similarly had gold trading near $4,366 to $4,405 depending on feed, as of the morning of September 10, 2026, so the two platforms' option-like ladders and the cash market are all telling the same story rather than diverging.

The one thing worth flagging for readers, not as an opportunity but as a caution, is how thin some of Polymarket's weekly "touch" contracts are. Several September-week low-touch markets (e.g., the $4,200, $4,150, $4,100 and $4,000 weekly buckets) show bids of just $0.02 against asks of $0.98 — a spread that wide is not a mispricing to exploit, it's a book with almost no resting liquidity, so the quoted mid is close to meaningless until someone actually trades near it. By contrast, the monthly Polymarket touch contracts and Kalshi's more actively traded strikes (volumes in the hundreds) have sensible, tight-ish spreads. Also worth remembering: Kalshi's contracts settle on the CME/spot fix at a specific time, while Polymarket's "touch" contracts pay out if price crosses the level at any point during the window — a genuine mechanical difference, not an error, and one reason the two venues' numbers for superficially similar strikes won't match exactly.
headline: Gold markets align near $4,350; no arbitrage found, but some Polymarket books are too thin to trust
